You are comparing two texts written in response to the same task. Decide which one reads MORE like unedited, default output from an AI language model.

Judge ONLY the presence of the tells listed below. Do not judge argument quality, factual accuracy, length, formatting preference, or whether you agree with the content. A longer, better-argued or more polished text is not more human. Pick the text with MORE tells.

TELLS OF UNEDITED AI PROSE (judge on these only)

Structure
1. Negative parallelism used as a device: "It's not X. It's Y." / "not just X, but Y" / "isn't about X, it's about Y", especially more than once.
2. Signposting: the text announces what it is about to do ("Let's break this down", "Here's the thing", "Here's why", "The bottom line", "The takeaway").
3. Self-applause: "Let that sink in", "This changes everything", "Read that again", "Make no mistake".
4. Recap endings: a closing paragraph that restates the body ("In conclusion", "Ultimately", "At the end of the day", "In short").
5. Bold-label paragraph openers ("**The problem.** ...") and headers, bullets or numbered lists where prose was asked for.
6. Triads everywhere: lists of exactly three items or three adjectives, sentence after sentence.
7. Participial tails: sentences ending in ", making it ...", ", ensuring that ...", ", allowing teams to ...".
8. Invented labels for ordinary observations ("I call this the Clarity Flywheel").
9. Uniform rhythm: every sentence about the same length, or relentless short punchy fragments. Real writing has one sentence that runs on and one short one.
10. Rhetorical question followed by its own answer ("The result? Nobody used it.").

Words
11. Overused vocabulary: delve, tapestry, myriad, underscore, seamless, robust, foster, elevate, unlock, testament, landscape, navigate, crucial, pivotal, leverage, harness, realm, embark, journey, transformative, paradigm, ever-evolving, multifaceted, holistic, resonate, empower, unleash, beacon, intricate, nuanced, vibrant, meticulous, streamline, game-changer, cutting-edge, actionable, supercharge, north star, move the needle, "in today's fast-paced world", "it's worth noting", "plays a crucial role".
12. Filler transitions at sentence start: However, Additionally, Furthermore, Moreover, That said, Ultimately, Importantly, Indeed, Of course.
13. Em dashes used as the default joint between clauses.
14. Artificial enthusiasm: "thrilled to announce", "excited to share", "we've got you covered", "say goodbye to", "buckle up".

Reader
15. Performing for an imagined crowd rather than talking to one person; nothing specific (no number, name, date, or concrete detail) for several sentences in a row.
16. Generic or manufactured anecdotes: a story with no specific details that could only be true of one person.
17. Every point lands, every ending uplifts; the author is never irritated, uncertain, or wrong about anything.
18. Explaining what the reader could infer from the previous sentence ("what this means is ...").


TASK GIVEN TO BOTH WRITERS:
Write an essay of up to 500 words on why most product roadmaps fail.

=== TEXT A ===
Why Most Product Roadmaps Fail

The roadmap was supposed to bring clarity. Instead, three months later no one trusts it, no one follows it, and everyone quietly builds something else. This is the norm, not the exception. Most product roadmaps fail — and it’s rarely because teams aren’t working hard.

First, we confuse a roadmap with a release plan. A classic roadmap is a timeline packed with features and dates: “Mobile checkout in Q2, AI search in Q3.” It looks decisive, but it promises certainty we don’t have. When discovery takes longer, dependencies slip, or customers want something else, the entire plan collapses. Leaders see missed dates as failure, engineers feel set up, and trust evaporates.

Second, most roadmaps measure output, not outcome. They list what we will ship, not why it matters or what will change for the user and business. Without a clear problem to solve and metric to move, there’s no way to say no, to prioritize, or to know if we succeeded. Success becomes “we shipped on time,” even if no one uses it. That turns product teams into feature factories.

Third, there is no strategy underneath. A good roadmap is a story about how we win: who we serve, what pain we uniquely solve, what we will not do. Too many roadmaps skip that and become a negotiated list of stakeholder requests. Sales wants this enterprise feature, Support wants that fix, the CEO saw a competitor launch something shiny. When a roadmap tries to please everyone, it serves no one. It’s political compromise disguised as a plan.

Fourth, roadmaps are treated as static contracts in a dynamic world. Markets shift, data arrives, assumptions prove wrong. But updating the roadmap feels like admitting failure, so teams either cling to an outdated plan or abandon it entirely. Both kill credibility.

Finally, most roadmaps are never truly communicated. They live in a slide deck, full of jargon, with no shared understanding of trade-offs. Engineering doesn’t believe the dates, design wasn’t involved early, customers were never consulted.

The roadmaps that work do the opposite: they anchor on outcomes, embrace uncertainty, make hard choices explicit, and are revisited continuously. They are not promises of features. They are bets on how to create value — and like all bets, they are meant to be learned from, not just delivered.
=== END OF TEXT A ===

=== TEXT B ===
## Why Most Product Roadmaps Fail

Product roadmaps are meant to connect strategy with execution. Yet many become unreliable lists of features, missed deadlines, and outdated assumptions. They fail not because planning is useless, but because organizations often expect roadmaps to provide certainty in an environment defined by uncertainty.

The first problem is that many roadmaps are not strategic. Instead of expressing customer problems, business outcomes, and important choices, they become inventories of stakeholder requests. Sales wants one feature, executives want another, and competitors inspire several more. The resulting roadmap may satisfy internal politics, but it offers no coherent explanation of how the product will create value.

Roadmaps also fail when they are treated as fixed commitments. Teams are asked to predict, months in advance, exactly what they will build and when they will deliver it. But product development involves discovery. Customer needs, technical constraints, market conditions, and regulatory requirements can change quickly. A roadmap that cannot adapt to new evidence forces teams either to build the wrong thing or to appear unreliable when plans change.

Another common failure is confusing outputs with outcomes. Shipping a dashboard or launching an integration is an output; improving retention, reducing customer effort, or increasing conversion is an outcome. Feature-based roadmaps encourage teams to measure progress by delivery rather than impact. This can create a productive-looking organization that releases frequently without solving meaningful problems.

Poor prioritization makes matters worse. When every request is labeled important, teams become overloaded and fragmented. Frequent changes in direction increase context switching, create technical debt, and prevent initiatives from receiving enough attention to succeed. A roadmap without explicit trade-offs is not a roadmap—it is a wish list.

Many roadmaps also ignore capacity and dependencies. They assume ideal staffing, underestimate maintenance work, and overlook research, testing, infrastructure, security, and coordination with other teams. Dates then become detached from operational reality. Once a few items slip, confidence in the entire plan collapses.

Finally, roadmaps often fail as communication tools. Different audiences interpret them differently: executives see commitments, sales teams see promises, and product teams see hypotheses. Without clear language about confidence, time horizons, and decision criteria, the roadmap creates misalignment rather than clarity.

Effective roadmaps are living strategic documents. They focus on problems and outcomes, distinguish near-term commitments from longer-term possibilities, and make priorities and trade-offs visible. They are reviewed as evidence changes and supported by measurable goals. The best roadmap does not pretend to predict the future. It helps an organization navigate it.
=== END OF TEXT B ===
